title: The sacred months
hook: four sacred months: Muharram, Rajab, Dhul Qa'dah, Dhul Hijjah (9:36)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the life cycle closed: carried, then carrying, then carried again. Today, a new stretch: the year itself.

The verse begins by counting. Surah al-Tawbah, in Pickthall's translation: "Lo! the number of the months with Allah is twelve months by Allah's ordinance in the day that He created the heavens and the earth." A calendar, built into creation. Then it marks some off from the others: "Four of them are sacred." It doesn't name them. For the names, you go to a sermon the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, gave at the farewell pilgrimage. Which four, and what makes a month sacred?
screen: `TWELVE MONTHS WITH ALLAH.` → `FOUR OF THEM ARE SACRED.` → `WHICH FOUR?`

segments.voice: You met some of these months one by one back in year two. Today, the frame that holds them. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Abu Bakrah reports the Prophet's words at the farewell pilgrimage, in paraphrase: the year is twelve months, and four of them are sacred. Three come one after another: Dhul Qa'dah, Dhul Hijjah and Muharram. The fourth stands alone: Rajab, the one between Jumada and Sha'ban. Three in a row, and one on its own. Back in al-Tawbah, right after "Four of them are sacred," the verse says: "So wrong not yourselves in them." Notice who gets protected. Not the month. You. Some commentators read it as saying wrongdoing weighs heavier in these months, the way a careless word lands harder in a holy place. So sacred time works like sacred space. A mosque is still a building, with walls and a floor, but you walk in differently. These four months are still ordinary weeks, with work and errands and laundry. The calendar says: walk in differently. Slower to quarrel. Quicker to do good. And because the months are named and fixed, nobody has to decide each year when to be more careful. The calendar decides. Over the coming days, the path walks through the year: Muharram, the other months Muslims keep, all the way to Ramadan and the Eids.
screen: `THREE IN A ROW, AND RAJAB ALONE.` · `SO WRONG NOT YOURSELVES IN THEM.` · `SACRED TIME, LIKE SACRED SPACE.` · `THE CALENDAR DECIDES FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: On each slow breath, say one name: Dhul Qa'dah, Dhul Hijjah, Muharram, then pause for the gap in the calendar, and say Rajab. Go round again, three and a pause and one, until the shape feels familiar. Then think of one place where you already walk in differently, a room, a grave, a kitchen table, and let the four months feel like that place.
The sacred months. Four of the twelve, named in the farewell sermon: Dhul Qa'dah, Dhul Hijjah, Muharram, and Rajab on its own. Times not to wrong yourselves. Today's word.
Your line: four sacred months. Three in a row, and one on its own. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1353 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: MUHARRAM: THE MONTH OF ALLAH.`

howItsDone: The Islamic calendar treats Dhul Qa'dah, Dhul Hijjah, Muharram and Rajab as sacred months, named in a hadith of the farewell sermon in al-Bukhari; Qur'an 9:36 asks people not to wrong themselves in them.

chat.says: Which months are sacred in Islam, and what's different about them?
options: Four, including Muharram and Rajab; the Qur'an says not to wrong yourselves in them.
Just Ramadan; the Qur'an says every other month is ordinary, with no rules.
Twelve; every month is sacred the same, so none is set apart at all.
chat.meaning: Qur'an 9:36 says four of the twelve months are sacred: Dhul Qa'dah, Dhul Hijjah, Muharram and Rajab. In them: wrong not yourselves.

al-Tawbah.meaning: the ninth surah of the Qur'an

Rajab.meaning: the sacred month that stands alone, before Sha'ban

Dhul Hijjah.meaning: one of the three sacred months that come in a row

Abu Bakrah.meaning: a companion who reported the farewell sermon's words
